**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Every bite of food you have ever eaten traces back to a plant catching sunlight. Today you find out exactly how that trick works — and why you are breathing because of it.

1. Read **The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf**. Notice the three ingredients and the two products.
2. Open the **Glossary** and win the **Word Scramble** — these words show up in everything else. Then win the **Memory** game.
3. Walk through **Follow One Carbon Atom** to see the order things happen.
4. Study the **Inputs and Outputs Map**, then try the sort: does each card go IN or OUT?
5. Take the quiz. It hunts for the two ideas almost everyone gets backwards.
6. Write your explanation with the **Sentence Frames**.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Sugar Factory** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Investigation: Which Light Grows a Plant?** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Read the **Four Things People Get Wrong** chart before the quiz — every one of those four is a common wrong answer.

One warning: two of the quiz questions are traps that catch even adults. Read carefully. 🌱☀️

Picture panels: Inputs and living leaves; Inside the leaf; Energy and respiration; Building living matter. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Sugar Factory** — study the example aid, then make one your own.

from:
## The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf

A tree standing in a field looks like it is doing nothing. It is actually running one of the most important chemical factories on Earth, and it is running on sunlight.

Here is the puzzle that confused scientists for centuries: where does the *stuff* of a tree come from? A giant oak weighs many tons. Does it eat the soil? In the 1600s, a scientist named Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a pot for five years. The tree gained about 74 kilograms. The soil lost almost nothing. The mass had come from somewhere else.

Most of it came from the **air**.

Inside every leaf are tiny green structures called **chloroplasts**, packed with a pigment called **chlorophyll**. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green — which is the only reason leaves look green to you. That captured light energy powers a chemical reaction. It has three ingredients, called **reactants**: **carbon dioxide** from the air, **water** from the roots, and light itself.

The reaction rearranges those atoms into two **products**: **glucose**, a sugar the plant uses for food and building material, and **oxygen**, which leaves through the same tiny pores that let carbon dioxide in. Those pores are called **stomata**, and a plant opens and closes them like windows — wide open to feed, squeezed shut when water is scarce.

So the oak tree is built, quite literally, out of thin air and water, assembled by sunlight.

Now the part that surprises people: plants also perform **cellular respiration**, the same process your cells use to release energy from sugar. Plants do it day and night. Photosynthesis is not the opposite of breathing — it is how the plant makes the fuel that its breathing burns. During bright daylight a healthy plant photosynthesizes much faster than it respires, so oxygen flows out on balance.

Every breath you take contains oxygen released by this reaction. Every calorie you eat, whether from broccoli or a burger, was originally sunlight captured by chlorophyll. Trace any food chain backward far enough and it always ends at a leaf, quietly turning light into life.

## The Sugar Factory in Every Leaf

A tree gains mass as it grows. Where does that new matter come from? Long ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow and found that it gained much more mass than the soil lost. This was evidence against the idea that the tree simply ate the soil. It did not identify every source of its matter.

Carbon in plant sugars and wood comes from carbon dioxide in the air. Water supplies matter too. Fresh plants contain a great deal of water, and they need mineral nutrients. Sunlight supplies **energy**. It does not turn into the atoms in wood.

**Photosynthesis** uses light energy to build sugars. In plant cells, it takes place in **chloroplasts**. These structures contain **chlorophyll**, a green **pigment** that absorbs light. Leaves absorb red and blue light strongly. They absorb some green light too. Some green light bounces off or passes through, helping leaves look green. Green light is not useless.

A simple equation shows carbon dioxide and water going in. They are material **reactants**. Light supplies energy, not atoms. Sugars and oxygen are **products**. **Glucose** is the sugar used in our simple equation. The real process has many steps. The released oxygen comes from water. The carbon in sugar comes from carbon dioxide.

**Stomata** are tiny pores. Guard cells control their openings. Gases move through them, but water can leave too. The pattern of opening depends on the plant and its conditions. Some plants take in much of their carbon dioxide at night.

Plants use sugars to grow and store material. They also use them in cellular **respiration**, day and night. One form of respiration uses oxygen and transfers energy from sugar into forms cells can use. It releases carbon dioxide and water. It is not the same as breathing.

Photosynthesis needs suitable light. A lamp can provide it as well as the Sun. In darkness, stored material can support growth and respiration for a while. Light-driven sugar production cannot continue without light.

A plant releases oxygen overall when photosynthesis makes more than respiration uses. Bright light alone does not guarantee this. Water, temperature and carbon dioxide also matter.

Many algae and some bacteria use photosynthesis too. It supports most familiar food webs. Some other ecosystems use energy from chemical reactions instead. Compare a bean plant, an oak and algae: what do they share, and what differs?

from: 7th Grade • Leveled reading
to: 7th Grade • Matter, energy and plant processes

from: The process plants use to turn light energy, carbon dioxide, and water into sugar and oxygen.
to: Using light energy to build organic matter. Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make sugars and release oxygen.

from: A substance that absorbs some colors of light and reflects others.
to: A substance that absorbs some colors of light more than others.

from: An ingredient that goes INTO a chemical reaction.
to: A material used in a chemical reaction. Light supplies energy rather than atoms.

from: The mass came from air and water
to: Carbon comes from carbon dioxide; water contributes matter and fresh mass includes water

from: NOT: "leaves are green because they use green light"
to: GREEN LIGHT CAN CONTRIBUTE

from: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue
to: Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in red and blue regions

from: It reflects green
to: Leaves reflect and transmit some green, and absorb some too

from: You are seeing the colour it refuses
to: Green light is not useless; conditions and intensity matter

from: Photosynthesis makes the fuel that respiration burns
to: Photosynthesis makes organic compounds; respiration transfers energy from them

from: They are not opposites
to: They are distinct linked processes, not the same as breathing

from: Glucose is the product the plant is after
to: Sugars support growth, storage and respiration

from: In bright light output beats use, so oxygen flows out on balance
to: Net oxygen output occurs when production exceeds use

from: Light energy + carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
to: Carbon dioxide + water → sugars + oxygen, powered by light

from: Inside the chloroplasts, in the leaf
to: In chloroplasts of photosynthetic plant cells

from: Reactants on the left, products on the right
to: Matter reacts; light provides energy

from: The reaction has three reactants: carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots, and light itself. It makes two products: glucose and oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. Plants also perform cellular respiration, day and night. Photosynthesis is how the plant makes the fuel that its breathing burns.
to: Carbon dioxide and water are material reactants; light is an energy input. Products include sugars and oxygen. Leaves absorb some green light as well as red and blue. Plant cells respire day and night; photosynthesis requires suitable light.

from: Three reactants in, two products out
to: Two material inputs plus light energy; sugar and oxygen outputs

from: Reactants (in): carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots, light energy captured by chlorophyll.
to: Material inputs: carbon dioxide and water. Energy input: light captured by pigments.

from: Most of a tree's mass comes from the carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
to: Carbon in plant sugars comes from carbon dioxide; water also contributes matter, and fresh mass includes water.

from: Chunk it 3-and-2. IN: Air, Water, Light. OUT: Sugar, Oxygen. Say 'three in, two out' and the numbers catch any missing ingredient.
to: Two materials plus light: carbon dioxide and water go in; sugars and oxygen come out.

from: Splitting the list into a chunk of three and a chunk of two turns five separate facts into two groups you can count on your fingers, and the count itself is a check.
to: The two materials supply matter. Light supplies energy. This is a summary of many steps.

from: Write the three reactants as one group and the two products as another.
to: Group the two material reactants, then add light as a separate energy input.

from: It reflects green light, which is the only reason leaves look green to you.
to: Leaves reflect and transmit some green light, and also absorb some green for photosynthesis.

from: Green is the REJECT. Chlorophyll keeps red and blue and throws green back at your eyes. What you see is what the leaf did not want.
to: Green light can bounce off, pass through or be absorbed. A green leaf can still use some green light.

from: The keyword REJECT flips the usual assumption (green must be what the leaf uses) into the correct one (green is what it reflects), and it sticks because it is surprising.
to: The three paths help explain both color and light use. Do not treat all green light as wasted.

from: Green is the ____. The leaf keeps ____ and ____ and throws back ____.
to: Some green is ____, some ____, and some ____.

from: Using your keyword, which color of light would be the worst for a plant?
to: Why can leaf color alone not tell us which lamp produces the most growth?

from: How does your keyword explain the FAQ about growing plants under red light?
to: How do reflected, transmitted and absorbed light explain both appearance and the limits of a growth prediction?

from: Pure green light is the worst choice for growing a plant, because that is the color chlorophyll reflects away.
to: Green light can contribute to photosynthesis and can penetrate into leaves and canopies. Equal lamp distance does not guarantee equal photon delivery.

from: In bright daylight a healthy plant photosynthesizes much faster than it respires, so oxygen flows out on balance.
to: A plant releases oxygen on balance when photosynthetic production exceeds respiratory use; conditions matter.

from: A leaf is a kitchen with a stove. Photosynthesis is cooking the meal from sunlight, water, and air. Respiration is eating it. You can only cook in daylight, but you eat all day and all night.
to: Think of a leaf as a light-powered workshop. Photosynthesis makes sugars. Respiration transfers energy from stored sugars to help run cells.

from: Cooking maps to making glucose, eating maps to releasing its energy, and the daylight rule maps to why photosynthesis stops at night while respiration keeps going.
to: The workshop is a comparison. Photosynthesis needs suitable light, including lamp light. Respiration goes on day and night.

from: Photosynthesis is like ____ a meal; respiration is like ____ it. Plants can only ____ in daylight, but they ____ all the time.
to: Photosynthesis uses ____ energy to build ____; respiration transfers energy from ____.

from: A bedroom plant will not steal your air at night; the amounts it takes in are tiny.
to: Plant cells continue respiration in darkness, using stored organic compounds. Photosynthesis and respiration are different cellular processes.

from: Inside a chloroplast, chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light energy from the Sun.
to: Chlorophyll and other pigments absorb light; leaves can use some green light as well as red and blue.

from: The atoms rearrange: water molecules are split, their oxygen is released, and the carbon and hydrogen are built into a glucose molecule.
to: Water is split in light-driven reactions, releasing oxygen; linked reactions incorporate carbon dioxide into organic compounds used to make sugars.

from: Reactants (what goes IN)
to: Inputs: material reactants and light energy

from: Plant mass comes mostly from air, not soil
to: Carbon in plant organic matter comes from carbon dioxide; water and minerals also matter

from: Goes IN (reactant)
to: INPUT (material or energy)

from: NEITHER (not a reactant or a product)
to: OTHER ROLE (in this model)

from: A 500-kilogram oak tree grew from a tiny acorn. Where did most of that mass come from?
to: Where did the carbon atoms in an oak tree’s wood mainly come from?

from: Chlorophyll absorbs green light most strongly
to: Chlorophyll absorbs green light more strongly than all other colors

from: Chlorophyll reflects green light instead of absorbing it
to: Some green light is reflected or transmitted; some is absorbed

from: Green is the color of glucose inside the leaf
to: Green is the color of the glucose stored inside the leaf cells

from: Leaves are dyed green by minerals from the soil
to: Minerals from the soil dye every part of the leaf bright green

from: Chlorophyll reflects green light instead of absorbing it
to: Some green light is reflected or transmitted; some is absorbed

from: Which list shows ONLY reactants of photosynthesis?
to: Which list contains the two material inputs and the energy input for the simplified photosynthesis process?

from: Van Helmont's willow gained 74 kg while the soil lost almost none. Explain what his experiment proved and what it did NOT prove.
to: What did van Helmont’s small soil-mass change suggest, and what could that experiment alone not establish?

from: It proved the tree's mass did not come from soil. It did not prove where the mass DID come from — he thought it was water alone, but most of it actually came from carbon dioxide in the air.
to: The small soil-mass loss did not account for the willow’s large gain, challenging the idea that the tree simply consumed soil. The experiment alone did not identify all matter sources or account fully for plant water content. Modern evidence shows carbon comes from carbon dioxide and water also contributes matter.

from: Photosynthesis needs three ingredients: ____, ____, and ____.
to: The two material inputs are ____ and ____; the energy input is ____.

from: Leaves look green because chlorophyll ____ green light instead of ____ it.
to: Green light can be ____, ____ or ____ by a leaf.

from: Most of a tree's mass comes from ____, not from ____, which we know because ____.
to: Carbon in wood comes from ____, while water contributes ____; sunlight supplies ____.

from: No — at night they stop photosynthesizing but keep respiring, so they take in a little oxygen and release a little carbon dioxide. The amounts are tiny; a bedroom plant will not steal your air.
to: Plants keep respiring in darkness. They take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis needs suitable light, which may come from the Sun or a lamp.

from: Those leaves have other pigments (like anthocyanins) layered over the chlorophyll. The chlorophyll is usually still there doing its job underneath.
to: Other pigments can make leaves look red or purple. Chlorophyll is often still present and working too.

from: Yes, surprisingly well. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue best, so red light works. Pure green light is the worst choice, because that is the color chlorophyll reflects away.
to: Yes, under suitable conditions. The amount of light reaching the leaves matters as well as its color. Equal lamp power or distance does not ensure equal useful light. Green light can help too.

from: Enormously. Tiny floating algae called phytoplankton run photosynthesis at massive scale and produce a huge share of Earth's oxygen — arguably more than rainforests.
to: Yes. Algae and some bacteria in the ocean use light to make organic matter and release oxygen. These tiny organisms help support ocean food webs. They are not all plants.

from: Mostly yes, and it sounds impossible until you know carbon dioxide is a gas made of solid-forming atoms. The carbon in wood was floating in the sky not long ago.
to: The carbon in sugars and wood comes from the air. But plants also contain water and matter from water and minerals. “Made of air” leaves out those parts.

from: Scientists are trying — it is called artificial photosynthesis. Copying what a leaf does cheaply and at scale turns out to be extremely hard, which is a good measure of how impressive leaves are.
to: Researchers study ways to use light to make useful fuels. A leaf gives us ideas, but a machine need not copy every step. Making a useful system at large scale is a challenge.

from: Design a fair test of how light color affects a fast-growing plant. Predict from what chlorophyll absorbs, control everything but the color, and decide what counts as evidence of photosynthesis.
to: Compare plant growth under specified light treatments. Record potential confounding factors and distinguish growth observations from direct measurements of photosynthesis.

from: The reading says chlorophyll absorbs red and blue and reflects green. An investigation lets students turn that into a prediction, then find out whether the plant agrees.
to: Pigment absorption motivates predictions, but leaf and canopy behavior and photon delivery also affect growth. The investigation tests treatments under recorded conditions.

from: A gardening club wants to grow lettuce indoors under colored LED strips to save electricity, and someone suggested green light because 'plants are green.' Your class has seedling trays, identical seeds, red, blue, green, and white LED strips, cardboard for light boxes, a ruler, and a scale.
to: A garden club wants to grow lettuce under indoor lamps. Someone suggests green light because plants look green. You have seeds, trays, red, blue, green and white LED strips, light boxes, a ruler and a scale. Compare the lamp setups for two weeks.

from: Which light color, or mix of colors, produces the most growth in two weeks, and does the result match what chlorophyll absorbs?
to: Under which lamp setup do the plants grow most in two weeks? What can this test tell us about light color?

from: Predict first from the pigment: chlorophyll absorbs red and blue and reflects green. Then design the test so that only the color changes.
to: Predict what will happen. Leaves can use some green light. To test color alone, also match the amount of useful light reaching the leaves. Lamp power and distance are not enough to prove a match.

from: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light most strongly and reflects green.
to: Leaves absorb strongly in red and blue regions and also absorb some green light; some green is reflected or transmitted.

from: Most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air.
to: Carbon in sugars comes from carbon dioxide; water also contributes matter and fresh mass includes water.

from: How will we keep water, temperature, and distance from the light the same for every tray?
to: How will we keep water, temperature, starting plants and hours of light the same?

from: What should we measure: height, number of leaves, weight, or color?
to: Will we measure height, leaf count or mass? What does each measure leave out?

from: How bright is each strip, and does brightness differ between colors?
to: Can we borrow a sensor to match the useful light at leaf level? If not, how will we explain that limit?

from: How many seedlings per color do we need so one unusual plant does not decide the result?
to: How will we use several seedlings so one unusual plant does not decide the result?

from: Only light color differs between trays; water, distance, and temperature are matched and recorded
At least four seedlings per color
Growth is measured the same way on the same days
The conclusion compares results to the prediction from chlorophyll's absorption and uses at least four glossary words
to: Use the same water, temperature, starting plants and hours of light.
Use at least four seedlings for each setup.
Measure in the same way on the same days.
If useful light is not measured and matched, compare lamp setups, not color alone.
Compare results with your prediction and use four glossary words correctly.

from: Two weeks of growing time
to: Two weeks of growing time.

from: Only the listed equipment
to: Use the listed tools; ask the teacher about a suitable light sensor.

from: Trays must be checked and watered every school day
to: Check and water trays every school day.

from: No claims beyond what the data shows
to: Height may show stretching, and fresh mass includes water. Neither directly measures how fast photosynthesis occurs.

from: A test plan, a prediction with its reason, a data table across two weeks, and a one-page recommendation to the gardening club that explains the result using the pigment facts.
to: Share a test plan, a prediction, a two-week data table and a recommendation. Explain the results and name what the test cannot show.

from: Which of your measurements shows photosynthesis happened, and which only shows the plant stretched toward light?
to: Which observations show growth or stretching, and why do they not directly measure photosynthetic rate?

from: Match everything but color. If the green tray also sat farther from its light, you learned nothing about color.
to: Equal distance and electrical power do not ensure equal photon delivery. Without that control, compare the tested lamps and disclose the limitation.

from: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is the only reason leaves look green to you.
to: Leaves absorb some green light as well as red and blue. To test spectrum, account for photon delivery, duration, plant conditions and the difference between growth and photosynthetic rate.
